name: Liquid silicone injection

card.summary: Injection of free liquid silicone under the skin to add permanent volume to areas such as lips, face, breasts or buttocks, a practice the US FDA does not approve for cosmetic use.
card.note: The FDA states injectable silicone is not approved for any aesthetic use; complications can appear years later and can be fatal.

quick.overview:
Liquid silicone injection places free silicone oil into soft tissue to create lasting volume. Those who choose it want fuller lips, a more defined face or larger curves without implants, and it has been used by physicians (in small microdroplet amounts for lips and scars) and, widely, by unlicensed injectors.

Medical literature mostly documents the complications: granulomas, migration, infections and, with large volumes, silicone embolism syndrome in the lungs. The FDA says injectable silicone is not approved for any aesthetic procedure, and a scoping review of illicit cosmetic injections found cases reported from 28 countries.
quick.how: The material is injected through a needle into the target area, either by a physician using medical-grade silicone in small amounts or by non-medical providers in so-called pumping parties or private settings. Results are visible immediately, and the volume is considered permanent because silicone is not absorbed. No technique, product or sourcing details are given here.
quick.risks: Reported harms include nodules and granulomas, chronic inflammation, skin changes, movement of the material to other body parts, infection, silicone embolism syndrome with breathing failure, and death. Problems can occur years after injection, even with medical-grade material in small amounts. Removal is difficult.

lead: Liquid silicone injection is the placement of free liquid silicone, a non-biodegradable polymer, into the soft tissue to add volume or fill depressions. People seek it for fuller lips, facial contouring, breast enlargement and buttock or hip augmentation, because it gives an immediate, lasting change in shape.[1][2]

Two very different uses exist. Physicians have used small amounts of medical-grade silicone for perioral rejuvenation, lip augmentation and scars, with one review describing 40 years of experience and recommending careful technique.[3] Separately, unlicensed injection of industrial or non-medical silicone has been reported worldwide, notably among transgender women seeking body contouring, and is linked to disfigurement, silicone pulmonary embolism and death.[2][4]
The US Food and Drug Administration states that injectable silicone is not approved for any aesthetic procedure, including facial and body contouring.[5]

chain: Silicone is injected into soft tissue
It stays in place as permanent volume
Fuller lips, cheeks or body curves
angle.text: Silicone adds volume where it is placed, producing an immediate and persistent change in lip, facial or body contour. The same permanence is why complications can appear long afterwards and are hard to reverse.

paras: Free liquid silicone differs from silicone gel breast implants or solid silicone implants because it is injected as a fluid and is not contained in a shell. It remains in the tissue and may provoke a foreign-body reaction.[6]
Cosmetic uses reported in the literature include lips, face, breasts, buttocks and legs.[1][3][7]

sections.h: Use in cosmetic and gender-affirming contexts
paras: A 2024 scoping review of illicit cosmetic injections screened 629 abstracts and included 142 citations from 28 countries; it found that roughly half of patients whose gender identity was described were transgender.[4] Reviews of gender-affirming care note that silicone injections for soft-tissue contouring are a medically unapproved route used by some transgender women, and that facelift may later be needed to treat cheek ptosis caused by silicone injections.[8][9][10]

A review in Facial Plastic Surgery Clinics of North America describes medical-grade liquid silicone for lip augmentation and perioral defects, reporting techniques developed over 40 years and combination with electrosurgery and shave excision where relevant.[3] Medical-grade silicone has also been injected in non-cosmetic settings such as foot padding in diabetic neuropathy and urethral bulking, in controlled trials.[11][12][13]

A 1975 JAMA series described migration, granulomatous hepatitis, hypopigmentation and death after silicone injections.[14] A 1996 series of 54 patients with problems after medical-grade silicone injection to the face and legs reported chronic cellulitis, nodules, foreign-body reactions and migration, often appearing many years later, even with good technique and small amounts.[15]

Silicone embolism syndrome, with breathlessness, fever, cough, haemoptysis and alveolar infiltrates, was reviewed in a 2005 case report comparing it with fat embolism.[16] Other reports describe late granuloma formation, pneumonitis in men injected subcutaneously, and an autoimmune-type picture after breast injection.[17][18][19] Imaging reviews note silicone migration after buttock injections.[7]

The FDA says injectable silicone is not approved for any aesthetic procedure and lists long-term pain, infection, scarring, permanent disfigurement, blood-vessel blockage, stroke and death among the risks. The agency's approved fillers are other materials, and non-absorbable fillers are approved only for nasolabial folds and cheek acne scars.[5]

Controlled data for cosmetic use are limited. A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 28 diabetic neuropathic patients gave silicone injections in the foot and reported outcomes at two years, but this was for plantar padding, not appearance.[11][12] A pilot of emulsified silicone with cross-linked hyaluronic acid has been reported as a filler combination.[20] Most cosmetic evidence consists of case reports, case series and reviews of complications.[14][15][16]

timeline.event: JAMA case series documents migration, hepatic granulomas and death after injectable silicone.[14]
Series of 54 patients with delayed complications after medical-grade facial and leg injections is published.[15]
Silicone embolism syndrome is reviewed alongside 32 hospitalised cases after illegal injections.[16]
Scoping review maps illicit cosmetic injection reports across 28 countries.[4]
